claims.text: Melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting of high-entropy alloys can be accurately determined by combining computational thermodynamics with experimental validation.
The starting materials are high-entropy alloys in the solid state at room temperature.
Computational models can predict the thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
Differential scanning calorimetry and X-ray diffraction can experimentally validate the predicted melting and fusion properties.
The proposed measurements use controlled heating rates in a laboratory environment.
Atomic interactions and phase stability are the structural factors governing the relevant thermodynamic behavior.
Computational models simulate the thermodynamic behavior of high-entropy alloys.
Experimental measurements provide empirical data with which computational predictions can be validated.
Computational predictions and experimental results are expected to differ by no more than 10%.
Current methods rely heavily on empirical data.
Current methods may not account adequately for complex interactions in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach applies specifically to high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach may not be valid for simpler alloy systems.
Limitations in computational-model accuracy and variability in experimental measurements can produce discrepancies between prediction and experiment.
